Same-different discrimination of English vowels

Source: R/data.R
vowel_discrimination.Rd

An AX discrimination task: listeners hear two vowels from different talkers and say whether they are the same or different. 20 native listeners of English and 30 L2 learners each hear six vowel contrasts, with 8 same and 8 different trials per contrast. Native listeners tell all contrasts apart; the learners only some of them. For signal detection theory: hits, false alarms, d' and response bias.

Usage

vowel_discrimination

Format

A tibble with 4800 rows and 7 columns:

listener

Listener ID, E01 to E20 (L1) and G01 to G30 (L2).

group

"L1" or "L2".

trial

Trial number in the listener's random order, 1 to 96.

contrast

Vowel contrast, named by lexical sets: "FLEECE-KIT", "FLEECE-DRESS", "START-STRUT", "TRAP-START", "THOUGHT-LOT" or "GOOSE-FOOT".

pair

Order of the two vowels: "AA", "BB", "AB" or "BA".

trial_type

"same" (AA, BB) or "different" (AB, BA).

response

"same" or "different".

Source

data-raw/vowel_discrimination.R

Details

True model: the differencing model for same-different designs (Macmillan and Creelman 2005). Each vowel gives a normal observation with SD 1; the two observations differ in mean by d on different trials and not at all on same trials. The listener says "different" when the absolute difference between them exceeds their criterion (mean 2, SD 0.35 across listeners). d is 3.9 to 4.6 for native listeners and 0.7 to 2.6 for learners, multiplied by a listener factor exp(skill) with skill normal, SD 0.2. With 8 trials per cell, hit rates of 1 and false-alarm rates of 0 are common, so the example adds 0.5 to each count and 1 to each number of trials; this correction pulls the native listeners' d' below their true values. The design follows the AX task of Georgiou and Giannakou (2024), whose learners discriminated FLEECE-DRESS and THOUGHT-LOT above chance and the other contrasts not; the listeners, d' values and responses here are simulated.

References

Georgiou, G. P. & Giannakou, A. (2024). Discrimination of second language vowel contrasts and the role of phonological short-term memory and nonverbal intelligence. Journal of Psycholinguistic Research, 53(1), 9. doi:10.1007/s10936-024-10038-z

Macmillan, N. A. & Creelman, C. D. (2005). Detection Theory: A User's Guide (2nd ed.). Mahwah, NJ: Erlbaum.

Examples

vd <- vowel_discrimination
vd$said_different <- vd$response == "different"
rates <- aggregate(said_different ~ listener + group + contrast + trial_type, data = vd,
                   FUN = function(x) (sum(x) + 0.5) / (length(x) + 1))
rates <- reshape(rates, idvar = c("listener", "group", "contrast"),
                 timevar = "trial_type", direction = "wide")
dprime_sd <- function(h, f) {
  if (h <= f) return(0)
  k <- sqrt(2) * qnorm(f / 2)
  uniroot(function(d) h - pnorm((k + d) / sqrt(2)) - pnorm((k - d) / sqrt(2)),
          c(0, 10))$root
}
rates$dprime <- mapply(dprime_sd, rates$said_different.different,
                       rates$said_different.same)
round(tapply(rates$dprime, rates[c("contrast", "group")], mean), 2)
#>               group
#> contrast         L1   L2
#>   FLEECE-KIT   3.55 0.91
#>   FLEECE-DRESS 3.48 2.83
#>   START-STRUT  3.17 0.88
#>   TRAP-START   3.72 1.36
#>   THOUGHT-LOT  3.45 2.20
#>   GOOSE-FOOT   3.20 1.09
